messages.subject_clean: Compute SE using LDSCoutput$V
messages.body_plain:
Just in case anyone else wants to get the SE from LDSC output (in gsem_obj), here's a function (adapted from the function used to report SE in the logfile, credits to my colleague Jacob Bergstedt):

compute_SE_of_rg <- function(gsem_obj) {

  S <- gsem_obj$S
  V <- gsem_obj$V

  ratio <- tcrossprod(1 / sqrt(diag(S)))
  S_Stand <- S * ratio

  scaleO <- gdata::lowerTriangle(ratio, diag = TRUE)

  #rescale the sampling correlation matrix by the appropriate diagonals
  V_Stand <- V * tcrossprod(scaleO)

  #enter SEs from diagonal of standardized V
  r <- nrow(S)
  SE_Stand <- matrix(0, r, r)
  SE_Stand[lower.tri(SE_Stand, diag = TRUE)] <- sqrt(diag(V_Stand))
  as.data.frame(as.matrix(Matrix::forceSymmetric(SE_Stand, "L")))

}

messages.subject_clean: Order of variables in zero-order sampling covariance
messages.body_plain:
I would simply specify a user model that estimates the genetic
correlation of interest. The SE of that rG will then be directly
output. See the STD_genotype portion of the output. This will be based
on the assumption that the h2 is fixed (i.e. it simply standardizes
the covariance relative to th h2, maintaining the p value of the
cov_g).

Alternatively, you can estimate the rG using a model that takes into
account the imprecision of the h2 estimates. This can be done achieved
by specifying a model along the following lines:

'
y1std =~ NA*y1
y2std =~ NA*y2

y1std ~~ 1*y1std
y2std ~~ 1*y2std

y1 ~~ 0*y1
y2 ~~ 0*y2

y1std ~~ y2std
'
In this case, the SE of the rG will not match the SE of cov_g from
S_Stand and perhaps be more similar to what you'd get if resampling
the rG estimates directly with the jackknife.

That said, here is the answer to your question about mapping the
elements of S to V.

On page 3 of the wiki, we show how to get the SEs of each element of S:

k<-nrow(LDSCoutput$S)
SE<-matrix(0, k, k)
SE[lower.tri(SE,diag=TRUE)] <-sqrt(diag(LDSCoutput$V))
In other words, the SEs (in V) corresponding to each element of S can
be mapped back to S by placing them into a matric that is the same
size of S.

We can use this same strategy to simply number each unique element of
S and map it back to the diagonal of V:
k<-nrow(LDSCoutput$S_Stand)
Snum<-matrix(0, k, k)
Snum[lower.tri(Snum,diag=TRUE)] <-1:(k*(k+1)/2)
Snum

To subset out the sampling covariance matrix for parameters of
interest simply refer to the locations of those parameters in V.
For instance, here I am interested in the elements representing the
covariance between variables 1 and 2 with variable 3, so I pull out
the locations within S that they correspond to:
elements=Snum[3,1:2]
Now I subset V based on those elements:
V[elements, elements]

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Within the recent paper by Andrew Grotzinger https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-022-01057-4
(which is great), it was proposed that ...

"EFAs were conducted for the genetic correlation structure derived from odd autosomes only. Confirmatory factor analyses (CFAs) specified on the basis of these EFAs were subsequently fit to a genetic correlation matrix estimated using only even autosomes. Using odd and even autosome covariance matrices for the exploratory and confirmatory models, respectively, provided a form of cross-validation to guard against model overfitting."

Is this really necessary/sufficient? Phenotypic variation and bias should be proportionally encoded across all autosomes, based on polygenic principles. Thus, the proposed even/odd sumstats would not be truly independent of each other. We can fit EFA/CFA using these different sumstats, of course, but I was interested in whether people ever found substantial differences using the even/odd split.

Thanks so much,
Beate

messages.body_plain:
The goal of splitting the analysis by odd and even autosomes is to
avoid overfitting to the observed covariance matrix given that it is
only an estimate of the population covariance matrix. Under a highly
polygenic model in which each biological pathways through which
variants operate is affected by many variants distributed across the
autosomes, we should expect approximately the same population model to
hold, so differences observed across odd and even autosomes should be
due to either overfitting to somewhat noisy estimates in the genetic
covariance matrix or to genuine differences in the pattern of genetic
sharing across odd and even autosomes.

This approach is based on the assumption that estimation error is
uncorrelated across autosomes (not that it is uncorrelated across
traits, which is handled by our use of multivariable LDSC), which is
essentially the same assumption on which the jacknife is based. Note
that the hold-out autosome strategy won't remove biases due to
failures of PCs and the LDSC model to fully control for pop strat and
assortative mating, but neither would using a hold-out sample of
individuals rather than autosomes.

To answer your question about our experience with this approach: Yes.
In ongoing work with a large number of GWAS traits, we have
encountered instances in which specific factor loadings that are
present in odd autosomes do not replicate in even autosomes. We treat
these specific loadings as having resulted from overfitting, and drop
them from subsequent models.

Hi Xavier,

The psych package that you used to run the EFA doesn't print the loadings if they are below a certain threshold, which is why it does not print the loadings for T1 and T2 when you run a single-factor EFA. The results are also sensible given that T1 and T2 are the specific traits that load on the second factor when you expand to run a two-factor EFA.

To your second question, it is certainly possible to test a hierarchical model like you've specified, and examine SNP effects on the hierarchical factor (L1).

Best,
  Andrew

messages.body_plain:
Hi Roya,

Great question! For pragmatic reasons, commonfactorGWAS only saves the SNP effects on the factor. Similarly, we always recommend using the 'sub' argument to specify which specific effects you want to save from the model (e.g., F1~SNP) so that you are not saving the full model output for every single SNP. The primary reason being that it will seriously increase the memory needs for the job if you save every single model parameter for each SNP. In addition, we not expect the parameters you highlighted in yellow to change very much for each SNP so it's often safe to assume that these values are approximately equivalent to the estimates you get when running the model using usermodel for the model without the individual SNP effects.

With all that said, I just put in a recent update to userGWAS this week to include a fix_measurement argument that tells the function to fix all of these estimates to improve interpretation, as each SNP can now be interpreted as going through the exact same measurement model. Their may be some instances where you want to see if the measurement model shifts for a particularly large effect SNP, in which case you can set fix_measurement to FALSE and not use the sub argument to get all of the model parameters. I'll be documenting this new fix_measurement argument in the coming weeks on the wiki, but hopefully this more generally answers your question for now.

Best,
  Andrew

messages.body_plain:
I misspoke about which approach assumes that h2 is "fixed" and want to correct it for the record.

When you estimate the genetic covariance in genomic SEM and look at the STD_genotype output (which, for a zero-ordered genetic correlation, is the same as looking at the relevant cell of S_Stand and corresponding SE^2 in V_Stand), you are obtaining and estimate and SE that assumes that genetic variances are *random*. In other words, even though the genetic variances are standardized to necessarily be 1.0, they still have SEs because this approach simply rescales the S and V matrices. The p value of the genetic correlation and genetic covariance will therefore match.

The alternative approache, code for which I provided in my last email (also below), specifies factors with *fixed* unit variances and therefore estimates rG in the unstanardized portion of the model itself. These factors are isomorphic with the genetic components of the original GWAS phenotypes, but rescale them to the standardized metric within the undstandardized portion of the model. In this case, the SE of the rG will not match the SE of cov_g from S and V (or from a conventional model that estimates cov_g without specifying factors with unit variances) and is likely to be more similar to what you'd get if resampling the rG estimates directly with the jackknife. In other words, this second approach treats the genetic variances as fixed since they have been rescaled to necessarily be 1.0.

Apologies for the confusion in the previous email.

'
y1std =~ NA*y1
y2std =~ NA*y2

y1std ~~ 1*y1std
y2std ~~ 1*y2std

y1 ~~ 0*y1
y2 ~~ 0*y2

y1std ~~ y2std
'

Hi, many thanks for this explanation and for sharing your findings!
My point was that it is not possible to adjust for all forms of bias by splitting the analysis into different chromosomes. Bias arises at the phenotype level and would equally apply to all chromosomes, making it undetectable. This seems to correspond to your answer. Also, bias may not always be fully removed with PCs and LDSC, even if methods are working accurately, as it may also involve e.g. recruitment or participation bias in addition to random sampling variation (out of a larger population). However, the split in odd/even is a clever workaround to adjust for bias as much as possible.

> Hi Roya,
>
> Great question! For pragmatic reasons, commonfactorGWAS only saves the SNP effects on the factor. Similarly, we always recommend using the 'sub' argument to specify which specific effects you want to save from the model (e.g., F1~SNP) so that you are not saving the full model output for every single SNP. The primary reason being that it will seriously increase the memory needs for the job if you save every single model parameter for each SNP. In addition, we not expect the parameters you highlighted in yellow to change very much for each SNP so it's often safe to assume that these values are approximately equivalent to the estimates you get when running the model using usermodel for the model without the individual SNP effects.
>
> With all that said, I just put in a recent update to userGWAS this week to include a fix_measurement argument that tells the function to fix all of these estimates to improve interpretation, as each SNP can now be interpreted as going through the exact same measurement model. Their may be some instances where you want to see if the measurement model shifts for a particularly large effect SNP, in which case you can set fix_measurement to FALSE and not use the sub argument to get all of the model parameters. I'll be documenting this new fix_measurement argument in the coming weeks on the wiki, but hopefully this more generally answers your question for now.
>
> Best,

Hi Izel,

Thanks for raising this! You are specifying the effects of gene expression on the factors correctly. It turns out this was a bug with a recent update to the userGWAS function that will fix the measurement model (factor correlations and factor loadings) prior to estimating the SNP or Gene effects on the factors. As an aside, the reason for this update is that it really speeds up the model estimation and it improves interpretability in so far as you know that the same exact model is being applied across all SNPs or genes.

The bug was that this update was coded to pick-up on estimate SNP effects in the model, but was a big oversight on my part that it should also be looking for Gene effects (as you correctly specified) in the model when TWAS=TRUE. I just put in an update that should fix this error if you could redownload the package and try your code after restarting R. The update also prints about this new fix_measurement update, which I plan to also have documented on the github wiki in the next week or so.

Unrelated to the bug you were getting, one thing I noticed about your model is that you have a single-item latent for F3. Since that part of the model is only defined by the one variable, you only have that variables variance (the SNP-based heritability) as the degree of freedom. Your model estimates both the factor variance and the the residual variance of FGlu, so the df is -1. To avoid this I would recommend adding the line below to the model that fixes the residual variance to 0 so that F3 can be interpreted as entirely defined by that indicator.

-Andrew
